## What the batch turned up besides definitions

Twenty-nine tasks drained in parallel — one reading and twenty-eight
definitions, all of the latter vocabulary that the 2026-09-06 readings
promoted. Three things came out of it that are worth more than the entries.

**A steering audit exists and nobody in this literature runs it.** Recorded as
a finding. *Evaluating the Semantic Specificity of Representation Steering*
applies a steering vector unconditionally to rule families the model already
handles above 95%, and a vector reported as a complete repair collapses
Llama-3.2-1B's native entailment accuracy from 99.6% to 40.4% — with no
strength recovering both, and with zero effect when injected during reasoning
tokens rather than at the final commitment, so it was a label bias rather than
a change of reasoning. Applied to length, the same shape would be a stop-token
bias: it would shorten traces on the target distribution while damaging
unrelated competence, and accuracy-plus-token-count reporting would not see it.
Checked against all nine steering-for-length readings the archive holds; ASC,
Reflection Steering and ERRV come close and none qualifies.

**Seven papers are held twice, and I made them.** Filing twelve PDFs by hand on
2026-09-06 created seven duplicate pairs: a `title:` record from a conference
virtual site and a `local:` record for the same paper, each read and answered
independently — once from an absent abstract, once from the document.
`dedupe conflicts` reports all seven and always did; running it before filing
would have prevented every one. The merge is left for a person: `local:` holds
the abstract, the document and the document-based reading in all seven cases,
so the direction is not in doubt, only the authority to make it irreversible.

**Roughly a quarter of authored `related` lists contain a dead link.** Of 322
records with a non-empty `related_authored`, 73 name at least one concept the
archive does not hold — 79 distinct names, 103 pointers. The worst are not
invented but mis-slugged: `optimalthinkingbench` (12 pointers) is real, filed
under the compound `optimalthinkingbench-overthinkingbench-underthinkingbench`;
`traac`, `pobs` and TALE are the same story. The long tail is genuinely
invented — `cifar-100`, `chinchilla-scaling-law`, `a-mousetrap` — mostly one
pointer each.

The instruction I have been giving every definition agent is part of the cause.
I told them to verify a neighbour with `ls data/concepts/<kebab-slug>.json`
before naming it, which is right in principle and wrong for this archive: entity
slugs are frequently compound, so the plain name of a real entity fails that
check. An agent that obeyed the instruction either dropped a good link or wrote
the plain name anyway. The check needs to search names and aliases inside the
files, not test a filename.
